extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism (undergraduate/graduate) and general readers interested in literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Applying New Criticism’s formalist method to analyze poems and prose: focus on the text itself through careful close reading, using formal elements and tensions to produce a single, unified interpretation while excluding authorial intent, reader response, and extratextual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading (explication de texte)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying a passage of prose or poetry requires careful, exacting scrutiny of the passage itself; close reading (or explication de texte) is a staple technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the words on the page meticulously. Focus analysis on diction, syntax, imagery, meter, rhyme, and other formal features of the passage rather than on external materials. The method rapidly became a standard pedagogical practice in U.S. universities for analyzing modern poetry and prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual autonomy / self-contained aesthetic object
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the work as a self-contained, self-referential aesthetic object — the text itself is the primary locus of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the literary work as autonomous: meanings should be located in the text rather than imported from outside (historical, biographical, or authorial sources). The movement 'emphasized close reading... to discover how a work of literature functioned as a self-contained, self-referential aesthetic object.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude author's intention (intentional fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on an author's intended meaning in analysis; the intentional fallacy holds that authorial intention is irrelevant to the text's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Wimsatt and Beardsley's principle that 'the words on the page were all that mattered' — avoid importing supposed authorial intent as evidence in interpretive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude reader's personal/emotional response (affective fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discount the reader's personal or emotional reaction as a valid basis for interpreting the text; the affective fallacy warns against equating response with meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ground interpretation primarily in individual reader experiences or emotional effects. The method treats such responses as potentially distracting from objective analysis of textual elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude historical, cultural, biographical, and moralistic contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to exclude historical and cultural contexts, biographical information about the author, and moralistic bias from the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New Critics argued that philological, historical, and biographical approaches 'distract from the text' and 'neglect its aesthetic qualities.' Keep extratextual materials from determining textual interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and meaning are intimately connected
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat structure/form and meaning/content as inseparable: structure and meaning should not be analyzed separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how formal elements (meter, rhyme, narrative structure, characterization, setting, etc.) instantiate and shape the poem’s or prose’s meaning; consider form and content together to account for the work’s effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal elements to identify theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Use formal features such as rhyme, meter, setting, characterization, and plot to identify the text's theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate patterns and interactions of formal devices as evidence for thematic claims. The article explicitly lists rhyme, meter, setting, characterization, and plot as tools New Critics used to identify theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek paradox, ambiguity, irony, and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify paradox, ambiguity, irony, and tension within the text to help establish interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices serve as evidentiary supports for a unified reading: New Critics 'looked for paradox, ambiguity, irony, and tension to help establish the single best and most unified interpretation of the text.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for a single best, unified interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to establish 'the single best and most unified interpretation' of a text rather than pluralistic or relativistic readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use close textual evidence and formal analysis to argue for a coherent, unified reading that resolves tensions and accounts for the work’s formal features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspiration to systematic, objective, precise criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate a newer, systematic, and (to some advocates) more objective or 'scientific' method of literary criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ransom and others urged that 'criticism must become more scientific, or precise and systematic.' While critics dispute the degree to which this is possible, New Criticism emphasizes rigor, precision, and methodical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern / common criticisms to avoid repeating
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and avoid New Criticism’s criticized tendencies: treating texts as wholly autonomous, ignoring social/human meaning, and dismissing ideological or historical readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argued New Criticism was 'uninterested in the human meaning, the social function and effect of literature' and that it could disguise interests at work in critical processes. Practitioners should note these limitations and the movement's inattention to feminist, post‑colonial, and other context-sensitive approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonality and objective correlative (influence from T.S. Eliot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Value the 'theory of impersonality' and the idea of the 'objective correlative' — poetry as impersonal and meaning produced by objective arrangements of images and symbols rather than by personal self-expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliot’s evaluative stance (condemnation or praise of certain poets, insistence that 'poetry must be impersonal') influenced New Critical canon formation; consider impersonality and objective correlative when justifying readings of poetic texts.
